title: Music Generation — MusicGen, Stable Audio, Suno, and the Licensing Earthquake

questions.question: A prompt asks for a 30-second instrumental loop. Which model family in the lesson predicts discrete audio-codec tokens?
options: A diarization and clustering pipeline
A mel-only classification network
An autoregressive token language model
A speaker verification embedding model
questions.explanation: MusicGen represents audio as discrete EnCodec codebook tokens and predicts those tokens autoregressively before decoding them to a waveform. A classifier assigns labels to audio; it does not generate a time-ordered sequence of codec tokens.

questions.question: A user hums a tune and wants a jazz-piano cover that preserves the melody but changes timbre. Which input path does the lesson describe?
options: MusicGen melody with a chromagram from the hummed audio
FAD reference folders passed to a codec decoder
Stable Audio Open with only a class label
Whisper timestamps attached to speaker embeddings
questions.explanation: MusicGen melody conditioning derives a chromagram from the hummed input and conditions generation on it, preserving the tune while changing timbre. FAD compares generated and reference audio distributions for evaluation; it is not a melody-conditioning input.

questions.question: How is FAD interpreted when comparing generated music with a reference set?
options: Lower embedding-distribution distance is better
Higher text-audio similarity distance is better
Lower transcription error means better FAD
Higher speaker similarity means better FAD
questions.explanation: FAD measures distance between generated and reference audio embedding distributions, so smaller distance indicates closer distributions. CLAP measures prompt-to-audio alignment as a separate score; FAD is a distribution distance where lower is better.

questions.question: When extending autoregressive MusicGen beyond roughly 30 seconds, what structural failure should you watch for?
options: Repetition or loss of musical structure over time
A codec format that cannot represent repeated notes
A loss of prompt text because FAD truncates the audio
A hard limit that prevents any output beyond 10 seconds
questions.explanation: Autoregressive MusicGen predicts codec tokens step by step and can repeat or lose structure as generation extends beyond about 30 seconds. The documented problem is repetition and structural drift, not a universal 10-second output cutoff.

questions.question: A sound-design task needs ambient textures and loops, with no full-song lyrics. Which stack is recommended?
options: Suno v5 for commercial full songs with vocals
ACE-Step XL for multilingual speech recognition
MusicGen melody mode for vocal separation
Stable Audio Open for instrumental sound design
questions.explanation: Stable Audio Open is the lesson’s choice for instrumental sound design, including loops and ambient textures without full-song lyrics. “Suno v5 for commercial full songs with vocals” targets a different task: generating complete vocal songs.

questions.question: A generated track scores well on FAD but seems off-prompt. What complementary evaluation should you use?
options: Report EER and speaker identity as the main music score
Add genre adjectives to prompts and compare FAD only
Measure CLAP alignment and review paired listener judgments
Repeat FAD with a smaller fixed reference collection
questions.explanation: FAD compares overall audio distributions, while CLAP checks alignment between a text prompt and its generated audio; listener judgments add a direct preference signal. EER measures speaker verification and cannot reveal whether the music matches its prompt.
